title: The Ten Commandments
lead: The Ten Words that God spoke at Sinai and wrote on two stone tablets (Exodus 20:1–17; Deuteronomy 5:6–21). They stand at the center of the covenant, and Jews and Christians number them in different ways.

sections.b: The Ten Words are given at Sinai (Exodus 20:1–17), written on stone tablets, broken after the golden calf and written again (Exodus 32:19; 34:1, 28), and repeated by Moses in Deuteronomy 5:6–21. The tablets were kept in the ark (Deuteronomy 10:1–5; 1 Kings 8:9). The prophets echo them when they accuse Israel of stealing, murder, adultery and lying oaths (Jeremiah 7:9; Hosea 4:2), and Psalm 81:9–10 repeats the first word. In the New Testament Jesus lists the commands of the second table (Mark 10:19), deepens them (Matthew 5:21–30), and sums up the law in love of God and neighbor (Matthew 22:37–40); Paul and James do the same (Romans 13:8–10; James 2:8–11).
sections.refs: Exodus 20:1–17; Exodus 34:28; Deuteronomy 5:6–21; Deuteronomy 10:1–5; Jeremiah 7:9; Hosea 4:2; Mark 10:19; Matthew 5:21–30; Romans 13:8–10; James 2:8–11

sections.b: In the Temple the Ten Words were recited daily with the Shema (Mishnah Tamid 5:1), until the rabbis stopped the practice so no one would say only these came from Sinai (Berakhot 12a). Synagogues today stand when they are read. Christian catechisms, Catholic, Lutheran, Reformed and Orthodox, teach the moral life through them, though they number them differently. In modern times they have also become a public symbol, and their display on public property has been fought over in the courts of the United States.
